body_markdown:
Asking me for career advice is like asking a groundhog for driving directions. Yet there I was this past weekend dispensing “wisdom” to my neighbor’s 20-year-old son. The kid is super bright and energetic, the exact opposite of what we so often hear these days, namely that kids are lazy and stuck in mom’s basement.


A college sophomore, he’s not sure what he wants to do but is already feeling pressure to pick a career path: If he doesn’t get the right internship next summer, he fears, he’ll be locked out of the good jobs he might want when he graduates. First off, damn this system that forces college kids to make such a momentous decision at the age of 20.


My previous career reviewing cars at *Car and Driver, Popular Mechanics* , and *Road & Track* looks awesome on paper, and it mostly was. But I got it by taking a huge gamble—ditching a salaried engineering job for a lowly $5 an hour gig at *Car and Driver* and white-knuckling poverty with credit-card debt. Timing and luck were every bit as important as the risks I took, so I’m reluctant to use my experience as any sort of road map.


My wife and I now have three kids about the same age as my young neighbor, so this topic of future careers is definitely top of mind in our household. We’re as confused as anyone. When it comes to guiding kids into needed and productive careers, we hear messages that seem to shift. Remember the once-loud cry that kids should “[learn to code”?](https://www.independent.co.uk/news/world/americas/ai-computer-science-degree-coding-teach-kids-b2855730.html) Now computer science majors[have some of the highest unemployment rates.](https://futurism.com/computer-science-majors-high-unemployment-rate) Whoops.


Leonard Ortiz/Digital First Media/Getty Images


The conventional wisdom that confuses me the most, however, is the idea that kids are not interested in science, technology, engineering, or math, the so-called STEM fields, prompting widespread calls for special programs to encourage STEM studies. Anecdotally, it does seem that there is a general lack of mechanical appetite among America’s youth, which speaks at least to the engineering part of STEM.


Since modern society no longer demands that folks mechanically engage with devices—we replace dishwashers rather than fix them—more and more households lack a DIY culture. My kids report that many of their friends don’t know which end of the screwdriver to hold. I’m not surprised—we live in a largely prosperous society and don’t need to make everything last for decades like previous generations did. What I hear from my kids and read is that few members of Gen Z are interested in STEM. Got it.


Ben Woodworth


Yet I see mountains of evidence that suggest the exact opposite. Consider the massive viewership of technical videos on YouTube. Last weekend I skipped Netflix to watch Dave Bell, owner and founder of Dave’s Auto Center,[dismantle a failed Land Rover V-8](https://youtu.be/CP_IIWkfc34?si=wI4TQgAiSHParGKO) and explain what went wrong with it. This is a highly geeky film that you might expect only a handful of super nerds like me would take the time to watch, but it had more than 750,000 views only ten days after it debuted.


Bell’s video is just one in a sea of highly popular videos that go deep into the technical weeds. Hagerty’s highest-viewed video is a[time-lapse rebuild of a Chevy Stovebolt engine](https://youtu.be/gJx4Ze-j348?si=aE6_hmBNL5C4Ih1v) that’s been viewed 52 million times.


Another data point, again anecdotal, is the vibrant technical world of[standalone engine computers.](https://www.hagerty.com/media/never-stop-driving/never-stop-driving-198-the-next-epidemic/) I’m installing one in a car I recently acquired, and since I’m in way over my head, I’m using YouTube and all the digital tools to learn everything from wiring to sensor specifications, programming, and even a little fabrication.


Lest you think this type of work is another niche, it’s not. There isn’t just one company that sells the computer, there are at least half a dozen, including Holley, Haltech, Link, Motec, and MaxxECU. Somebody’s buying all this stuff. I’ve found plenty of message boards and groups that share information and advice. The people I’ve observed are teaching themselves for the dopamine hit of tactile, amateur problem-solving. For my part, I’m learning more than I ever did during the four years I spent at engineering school.


One final data point: My youngest, who’s still in high school, hangs with the sort of grease monkeys many of you might recognize. His group of car tinkerers recently pooled their money to buy a used single-cylinder[Predator](https://www.harborfreight.com/brands/predator/engines.html) engine just so they can rebuild it. Even if “rebuild it” might amount to “take it apart, scratch heads, and admit defeat,” it’ll be time well spent. The tinkering is the point.


Getty Images


All this leads me to think that interest in engineering and the mechanical arts is stronger than ever. Clearly, legions of passionate people, young and old, are searching for ways to scratch their builder’s itch. So why the constant hand-wringing about STEM?


If there’s a finger to point, I direct one at our society’s demand for accreditation. Many companies rely on colleges and universities to filter out prospective hires, with the rationale that earning a degree proves someone is reasonably intelligent and can follow through. I wonder, however, if that forces too many people into an education system that poorly suits them. I consider myself in that camp.


Engineering college was so painfully boring that it nearly drummed out my natural mechanical curiosity. I would have dropped out of school entirely, but I knew I needed that piece of paper, the degree. And I was right—the head honcho at *Car and Driver* responded to my request for an internship by saying, “We’ll definitely take a Lehigh engineer for five bucks an hour.” Ahh, but the joke was on him! Little did he know that I knew nothing.


Finn Gomez/The Boston Globe/Getty Images


So, what if all those folks watching technical videos and building ECUs have had the courage I lacked 35 years ago? What if they bypassed the university gatekeepers entirely, trading the dry theory of the lecture hall for the unaccredited garage? Might that have led educators and commentators to miss the point and conclude that the problem is in interest rather than in how we educate?


Back in my garage with my 20-year-old neighbor, I told him that there is no single solution. My career happened simply because I was lucky enough to have a North Star to follow: my interest in cars. Few are blessed with such a passion, I said, so beware of the baloney bromides that set unrealistic expectations like “Do what you love, and you’ll never work a day in your life.” My go-to for these situations is Mike Rowe, the host of the TV show *Dirty Jobs* .[I shared this video](https://youtu.be/-KF0AN4H3U8?si=McwCaDw8MdVOhCIe) in which Rowe dispenses common-sense wisdom based on spending hours with folks doing what many consider society’s worst jobs yet, he claims, are happier than most.


I’m curious to know your thoughts on this complicated topic, so please comment down below.
